strengths: The paper identifies a clean and useful product-geometry view of the Cholesky manifold and leverages it to derive Power-Cholesky and Bures-Wasserstein-Cholesky metrics with many closed-form operators. The construction is mathematically natural and potentially useful for SPD learning.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat incremental: the key idea is to replace the diagonal scalar geometry inside an already-known Cholesky pullback framework. The contribution is elegant, but the conceptual leap over Log-Cholesky and power-deformed SPD metrics is moderate rather than major.

Some theoretical claims appear overstated. In particular, the gyrovector-space results rely on positivity/domain assumptions for the operations, and inverses are not globally defined on the full manifold. The paper sometimes states full gyrovector-space structure despite only having locally or conditionally defined operations, with later numerical clipping suggested as a remedy.

The experimental comparison may be partly affected by hyperparameter selection. The deformation parameter theta is selected from broad sweeps, but it is not clear that this tuning is done with a proper validation protocol rather than implicitly optimizing reported test performance.

The residual-block evaluation is relatively thin: it reports only theta-PCM, omits theta-BWCM, gives best-of-three results rather than mean/std, and uses fewer details than the classifier experiments.

The numerical-stability experiment is synthetic and somewhat favorable to the proposed metrics; it demonstrates overflow/NaN avoidance for extreme diagonal values, but does not fully establish that this is the dominant failure mode in real SPD networks.

Reproducibility and presentation have notable issues: the abstract has a blank code URL, the reproducibility statement says code will be released only upon acceptance, a footnote for SPD MLR code is blank, and the appendix contains an unbuilt glossary error message. These are fixable but unpolished for a top-tier submission.

strengths: The paper identifies a simple product decomposition of the Cholesky manifold and uses it to derive closed-form operators for two families of Cholesky-induced SPD metrics. This is a coherent and potentially useful direction for SPD neural networks.
The proposed metrics are computationally attractive: they avoid eigendecompositions in the main operators and inherit the practical efficiency of Cholesky-based methods.
The empirical section covers several SPD-learning settings, including MLR classifiers, residual blocks, numerical stability experiments, interpolation, scalability, and deformation-factor ablations.
The appendices include derivations and implementation details, which helps clarify how the proposed operators are obtained and applied.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. Much of the construction follows almost directly from product geometry, scalar SPD metrics, and pullback through Cholesky decomposition. The resulting metrics appear more like a useful reparameterized family of Cholesky metrics than a conceptually strong new geometric contribution.

A central theoretical claim is overstated: the gyrovector-space theorem is problematic because the proposed gyroaddition and gyromultiplication are only locally/partially defined under positivity constraints. A gyrogroup/gyrovector space normally requires total operations on the set, so stating that the whole Cholesky/SPD manifold satisfies the axioms is not justified. The suggested numerical clipping workaround does not preserve the claimed algebraic structure.

The evaluation appears hyperparameter-biased. The deformation parameter theta is selected from sweeps reported on the same benchmark results, with no clear validation split or nested selection protocol. This makes the headline accuracy gains difficult to interpret fairly.

The experimental comparisons are incomplete. Main classification results compare mainly against AIM, LEM, and LCM, while PEM, BWM, GBWM, and other relevant Cholesky/power baselines are mostly absent from the main task evaluation despite being discussed as related metrics.

The claimed numerical-stability advantage is based on synthetic geodesic failure tests that are favorable to the proposed diagonal-power operators and do not convincingly establish robustness in realistic end-to-end training. The paper also admits failures as theta approaches the log metric, but the practical stability/accuracy trade-off is not rigorously characterized.

The empirical gains are not consistently strong across all settings; some improvements are modest, and BWCM is not clearly better than baselines in several cases. Residual-block experiments report best results over three trials rather than robust mean/std comparisons.

The use of Cholesky decomposition makes the geometry coordinate/order dependent, but the paper does not sufficiently discuss the implications of this lack of congruence/permutation invariance for SPD learning tasks.

Reproducibility and polish are weak for a top-tier submission: the abstract says code is available but no URL is provided, the appendix contains an unresolved glossary build error, and some tables/formulas have formatting or apparent typographical issues. These issues reduce confidence in the care of the submission.

Overall, while the paper is understandable and has some useful engineering ideas, the contribution seems incremental, the strongest theoretical claim is not sound as stated, and the empirical evidence is not clean enough to support acceptance at a top-tier AI venue.

strengths: The paper identifies a clean product-geometry view of the Cholesky manifold and uses it to derive two SPD metrics with closed-form geodesics, logarithm/exponential maps, parallel transport, Frechet means, and gyro-operations. This is mathematically elegant and useful for SPD learning.

The proposed PCM and BWCM are practically motivated: they preserve the computational advantages of Cholesky-based geometry while replacing diagonal log/exp operations with power-based alternatives that can improve numerical stability.

The experimental section is fairly broad for this subarea, covering SPD MLR classifiers, GyroSPD, Riemannian residual blocks, synthetic stability tests, tensor interpolation, deformation-factor ablations, scalability, and the role of the diagonal matrix M.

Results are consistently favorable across the main SPD learning benchmarks, with meaningful accuracy gains over LCM/AIM/LEM in several settings and clear runtime advantages over eigendecomposition-heavy metrics.
The appendix contains proofs, notation, implementation details, hyperparameter sweeps, and additional analysis, making the theoretical and empirical story easier to audit.
weaknesses: The novelty is solid but somewhat incremental: the construction is largely a principled recombination of known Cholesky pullbacks, 1D SPD metrics, power deformations, and existing SPD network modules. The paper is more a strong metric-engineering contribution than a conceptual breakthrough.

Empirical fairness is a concern. The proposed methods benefit from an explicit sweep over theta, with the best values reported, while it is less clear that all baselines receive comparable hyperparameter tuning or analogous preprocessing choices. This makes some accuracy gains harder to attribute solely to the new geometry.

The strongest empirical claims are concentrated on a small set of standard SPD benchmarks. Broader validation on additional domains, larger modern architectures, or downstream tasks where SPD geometry is central would strengthen the impact case.

The stability experiment demonstrates overflow/NaN robustness for geodesic computations, but it is somewhat synthetic and tailored to the claimed weakness of diagonal log metrics. More task-level evidence under ill-conditioned real data would make the robustness claim more convincing.

Some practical aspects remain underdeveloped: the code is promised but not currently available, and the paper does not fully discuss sensitivity, model-selection cost for theta, or how practitioners should choose theta without validation sweeps.

Presentation has minor but visible issues, including a broken glossary/acronym build artifact and some cramped tables. These do not undermine the contribution, but they suggest the manuscript needs polishing before publication.
